common_name: Bonbon Squash (AAS-Winning Sweet Early Buttercup-Type Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Bonbon is an AAS-winning buttercup-type winter squash bred for earlier ripening and more compact vines than standard buttercup squash, with exceptionally sweet, dense orange flesh.

directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Bonbon is an AAS-winning improvement on the classic buttercup winter squash, ripening earlier and growing on a more compact vine than standard buttercup types while producing the same dark-green, turban-shaped fruit with a distinctive gray-blue button on the blossom end. The dense, deep-orange flesh is notably sweet and dry-textured, excellent baked, mashed, or used in place of pumpkin in pies and soups. Its earlier maturity is a real advantage in areas with a shorter warm season or where gardeners want to fit squash into a tighter succession-planting schedule. Fruit is ready to harvest when the rind hardens and the stem begins to dry and corky; cure harvested squash in a warm, dry spot for one to two weeks before storing to improve flavor and shelf life.

planting.note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Butterscotch is an AAS-winning personal-size butternut squash on compact semi-bush vines, bred for notably sweet flavor and a manageable single-serving fruit size.

directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Butterscotch is an AAS-winning butternut-type squash bred for a compact, semi-bush vine and small, personal-size fruit — about a pound each, roughly half the size of standard butternut squash — making it easy to fit multiple plants into a smaller garden and giving perfectly portioned single-serving squash for roasting or stuffing without leftovers. The tan-skinned, elongated fruit has dense, sweet, deep-orange flesh with the classic butternut flavor, and its smaller size means faster cooking too. Fruit is ready to harvest when the rind hardens fully and turns a deep tan color; cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two after harvest to improve flavor and storage life. Watch for squash vine borer and squash bugs, common problems on all winter squash in the Gulf South.

common_name: Sugaretti Squash (AAS-Winning Compact Sweet Spaghetti Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Sugaretti is a compact, bush-habit spaghetti squash bred for sweeter flavor than standard spaghetti squash on a vine that takes much less space to grow.

directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or grow in a large container. Sugaretti is an AAS-winning spaghetti squash bred for a genuinely compact, bush-type habit that fits into much smaller garden spaces than traditional sprawling spaghetti squash vines, while also improving on the flavor of standard spaghetti squash with noticeably sweeter, less bland flesh once the strands are separated after cooking. The fruit is a good single-family size, with pale-yellow, oval, ridged rind. Fruit is ready to harvest when the rind hardens fully and turns a deep golden-yellow; cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two after harvest before storing or cooking. Roast, bake, or boil the whole squash, then scrape the cooked flesh with a fork to separate it into spaghetti-like strands.

common_name: Harvest Moon Watermelon (AAS-Winning Seedless Icebox Watermelon)

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after soil warms to 70F and all frost danger passes; Harvest Moon is an AAS-winning seedless watermelon bred for extra sweetness and very uniform, round, icebox-size fruit. Plant alongside a seeded pollinizer variety, since seedless watermelons need pollen from a seeded type to set fruit.

directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after soil warms, and plant a seeded watermelon variety nearby to supply the pollen seedless watermelons need to set fruit. Harvest Moon is an AAS-winning seedless watermelon bred for very uniform, round, icebox-sized fruit — a manageable size for a refrigerator, unlike the largest field watermelons — with exceptionally sweet, crisp, deep-red flesh and only small, soft, edible white seed traces rather than the hard black seeds of standard watermelon. Its consistent size and shape make it a strong choice for home gardeners who want reliable, high-quality fruit without needing to manage a huge sprawling harvest. Watermelons need deep, well-drained soil and consistent irrigation through fruit development; drought stress during fruit fill reduces size and quality. Judge ripeness by the ground spot turning from white to yellow and a dull, hollow thump when the fruit is tapped.

common_name: Sweet Favorite Watermelon (AAS-Winning Classic Striped Picnic Watermelon)

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after soil warms to 70F and all frost danger passes; Sweet Favorite is a long-standing AAS-winning watermelon prized for exceptional sweetness on a large, classic oblong striped fruit good for feeding a crowd.

directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after soil warms. Sweet Favorite is a long-established AAS-winning watermelon, producing large, oblong, classically striped fruit in the traditional picnic-watermelon style, prized above all for exceptional sweetness that has kept it a favorite for decades since its introduction. Fruit commonly reaches 15-25 pounds with crisp, bright-red flesh and a good, thin-but-sturdy rind for handling and short-term storage. Its large size makes it well suited to feeding a crowd at a summer gathering, in keeping with its classic picnic-watermelon role. Watermelons need deep, well-drained soil, ample space, and consistent irrigation through fruit development, since drought stress during fruit fill causes smaller fruit and hollow heart. Judge ripeness by the ground spot yellowing, the tendril nearest the fruit drying and curling, and a dull, hollow thump when tapped.

common_name: Golden Crown Watermelon (AAS-Winning Yellow-Rind Icebox Watermelon)

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after soil warms to 70F and all frost danger passes; Golden Crown is an AAS-winning early, compact icebox watermelon whose rind ripens to solid golden-yellow instead of green, giving an easy visual ripeness cue unlike most watermelons.

directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after soil warms. Golden Crown is an AAS-winning early, compact icebox-type watermelon with an unusual and genuinely useful feature — the rind ripens from green to a distinctive solid golden-yellow at full maturity, giving gardeners a clear, unmistakable visual cue for ripeness instead of relying only on the ground-spot color, tendril drying, and thump-sound methods needed for green-rind watermelons. Inside, the flesh is sweet and red, with a compact plant habit and fast maturity that suit smaller gardens and shorter growing seasons well. Watermelons need deep, well-drained soil and consistent irrigation through fruit development for the best size and flavor; ease off watering slightly as fruit nears full color to help concentrate sugars.
sources: All-America Selections — Golden Crown Watermelon winner announcement
